title: Generalising Kernelised Gradient Flows
text:
Overview and Goals

By a kernelised gradient flow, I precisely mean something like: 
\partial_t q = -\nabla\cdot\left(q \, \mathcal{K}_q \nabla \frac{\delta \mathcal{J}}{\delta q} \right),
 where q is a PDF, \partial_t q = -\nabla\cdot\left(q \nabla \frac{\delta \mathcal{J}}{\delta q} \right) defines a continuity equation, \mathcal{J} is a functional defined over distributions, and \mathcal{K}_q is a kernel operator: 
\mathcal{K}_q v = \int K(x,\cdot) v(x) \,\mathrm{d}q(x).

This defines a gradient flow over a Riemannian manifold of probability measures. Precisely: Otto’s Wasserstein space W_2 with its tangent spaces restricted to an RKHS: 
T^{(K)}_q \mathcal{P}_2 = \{ - \nabla\cdot(q \varphi) \mid \varphi \in \mathcal{H}_K \}.


Goals of the talk:

Present a brief intro/review of different Kernelised Gradient Flows.
Present potential avenues of future research (e.g. discrete analogues).

title: Generalising Kernelised Gradient Flows
text:
Intuition Building
Suppose we want to minimise an objective

\mathcal{J} : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}.

To define a flow (a continuous-time optimisation), we only need two ingredients:

Allowed directions. Which way can we move from a point x \in \mathcal{X}?
→ This defines the tangent space or “neighbourhood structure” around x.
Cost of motion. How expensive is it to move a small amount in a given direction?
→ This defines a local metric, measuring infinitesimal displacement cost.

Together, these determine the geometry of the space.
Once we have geometry, a flow is simply “move downhill as fast as possible given that geometry”: 
  \dot{x}_t = -\,\operatorname{grad}_{g}\mathcal{J}(x_t).

title: Generalising Kernelised Gradient Flows
text:
Flows on Riemannian Manifolds
A Riemannian manifold (\mathcal{M}, g) gives us exactly the two ingredients we need:

Allowed directions:
→ The tangent space T_x\mathcal{M} specifies all directions we can move from x.
Cost of motion:
→ The Riemannian metric g_x : T_x\mathcal{M} \times T_x\mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R} assigns an inner product to each tangent space.

Given an objective \mathcal{J}:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}, its differential at x\in\mathcal{M} is: 
D\mathcal{J}(x) : T_x\mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}, \quad
D\mathcal{J}(x)[v] =
\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\,\mathcal{J}(\gamma(\varepsilon))\right|_{\varepsilon=0},
 where \gamma is any smooth curve in \mathcal{M} with \gamma(0)=x and \dot{\gamma}(0)=v.

So D\mathcal{J}(x)\in T^*_x \mathcal{M} and D\mathcal{J}(x)[h] \in \mathbb{R} is the directional derivative of \mathcal{J} in direction h\in T_x\mathcal{M}.
The metric g defines the Riemannian gradient 
g_x(\operatorname{grad}_{g}\mathcal{J}(x), v) = D\mathcal{J}(x)[v],\quad \forall \, v\in T_x \mathcal{M}

The Riemannian gradient defines the flow 
\dot{x}_t = -\,\operatorname{grad}_{g}\mathcal{J}(x_t).

title: Generalising Kernelised Gradient Flows
text:
Example: Euclidean Space
\mathbb{R}^d equipped with the metric g_x(u, v) = u^\top v defines a Riemannian manifold.

Objective and Differential: Given an objective \mathcal{J}, its differential is the Euclidean total derivative 
D\mathcal{J}(x) = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac{\partial}{\partial x_1} \mathcal{J}(x), \ldots, \tfrac{\partial}{\partial x_d} \mathcal{J}(x)  \end{pmatrix}.

Metric inverse (Onsager Operator): The metric defines an isomorphism between the tangent and cotangent spaces: 
g_x : T_x\mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow T_x^*\mathbb{R}^d,
\qquad
g_x(u) = u^\top,
 with inverse 
g_x^{-1} : T_x^*\mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow T_x\mathbb{R}^d.
 Applying g_x^{-1} to the differential gives the Riemannian gradient: 
\operatorname{grad}_g \mathcal{J}(x)
= g_x^{-1}(D\mathcal{J}(x))
= \nabla \mathcal{J}(x) =
\begin{pmatrix}
\tfrac{\partial \mathcal{J}}{\partial x_1} \\
\vdots \\
\tfrac{\partial \mathcal{J}}{\partial x_d}
\end{pmatrix}.

Gradient Flow: The gradient flow is 
  \dot{x}_t = -\,\nabla \mathcal{J}(x_t).

title: Generalising Kernelised Gradient Flows
text:
Example: Wasserstein Space
Let \mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d) denote the Wasserstein–2 space of probability densities with finite second moments. When endowed with the Otto Riemannian structure, it becomes an (infinite-dimensional) Riemannian manifold.
Motivation: Otto’s construction is based upon the Benamou and Brenier characterisation of Wasserstein 2-distance:

W_2(\rho_0, \rho_1)^2 = \inf_{\rho_t, v_t} \int_0^1 \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \|v_t(x)\|^2 \rho_t(x) \, \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}t

with \rho_t and v_t constrained to follow the continuity equation

\partial_t \rho_t = -\nabla\cdot(\rho_t v_t), \quad \rho_{t=0} = \rho_0,\; \rho_{t=1} = \rho_1.


Tangent space:
The tangent space at \rho \in \mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d) is the L^2(\rho)-closure of smooth velocity fields, modulo divergence-free components:

  T_\rho \mathcal{P}_2
  \;=\;
  \overline{
  \{\, \nabla \phi : \phi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d) \,\}
  }^{\,L^2(\rho)}.
   Each tangent vector \xi can be represented as

  \xi = -\,\nabla \!\cdot (\rho v),
  \quad v \in L^2(\rho; \mathbb{R}^d),
   where v is defined up to \rho-divergence-free components.
Objective and Differential: Given

title: Generalising Kernelised Gradient Flows
text:
Research Ideas

Consider more general objectives: As we saw, not all continuity equations correspond to a Fokker-Planck Equation. In general, they would correspond to a McKean-Vlasov SDE (i.e. a mean-field Markov process). This setup underlies SMC…
General Markov Processes: A general (Levy) Markov process consists of a drift, diffusion and a jump: 
\mathcal{J}f = f + \nabla + \int g ...
 Including jumps still defines a valid Stein operator! Does a gradient flow make sense here?
Discretise Time: Almost all MCMC methods used in practice discretise time and correct this discretisation error via an accept-reject scheme.
Discretise Space: Pretty sure that SVGD has only ever been constructed over continuous space!

title: Generalising Kernelised Gradient Flows
text:
Discretising Space
In order to deal with discrete scenarios, we require the notion of a gradient flow in discrete space.
The paper “Gradient flows of the entropy for finite Markov chains” by Jan Maas provides precisely this construction, defining a Wasserstein-type Riemannian manifold structure over discrete (finite) state spaces.
Setting
Let the state space be a finite set X, and let K(x,y) denote the transition probabilities of an irreducible, reversible Markov kernel with stationary measure \pi satisfying detailed balance: 
\pi(x) K(x,y) = \pi(y) K(y,x) \quad \forall\, x,y \in X.

We work with densities with respect to \pi: 
\mathcal{P}(X) = \left\{ \rho : X \to [0,\infty) \;\middle|\; \sum_{x \in X} \pi(x)\rho(x) = 1 \right\}.

Entropy Functional
The analogue of the continuous entropy functional is the relative entropy 
\mathcal{H}(\rho) = \sum_{x \in X} \pi(x) \, \rho(x) \log \rho(x).

The goal is to define a metric on \mathcal{P}(X) such that the heat flow associated with K is the gradient flow of \mathcal{H}.
Continuity Equation on a Graph
A curve (\rho_t)_{t \in [0,1]} in \mathcal{P}(X) satisfies the discrete continuity equation 
\frac{d}{dt}\rho_t(x)
+ \sum_{y \in X} (\psi_t(y) - \psi_t(x))\, K(x,y)\, \rho_t(x,y)
= 0,
 where \psi_t : X \to \mathbb{R} plays the role of a potential function, and 
\rho_t(x,y) = \theta(\rho_t(x), \rho_t(y))
 is a symmetric edge-density function, typically taken to be the logarithmic mean 
\theta(s,t) =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{s - t}{\log s - \log t}, & s,t > 0,\, s \neq t,\\[1.2em]
s, & s = t.
\end{cases}

This discrete continuity equation is the analogue of \partial_t \rho + \nabla \cdot (\rho \nabla \psi) = 0 in the continuous Benamou–Brenier formulation.
Discrete Wasserstein Metric
The Maas metric W between two densities \rho^0, \rho^1 \in \mathcal{P}(X) is defined via a discrete Benamou–Brenier formula: 
W(\rho^0, \rho^1)^2
=
\inf_{\substack{(\rho_t, \psi_t) \\ \rho_0 = \rho^0,\, \rho_1 = \rho^1}}
\int_0^1
\frac{1}{2}
\sum_{x,y \in X}
(\psi_t(x) - \psi_t(y))^2
\, K(x,y)\, \rho_t(x,y)\, \pi(x)
\, dt,
 subject to the discrete continuity equation above.
Riemannian Structure
At a fixed \rho \in \mathcal{P}(X), the tangent space T_\rho \mathcal{P}(X) consists of discrete gradients of potentials \psi : X \to \mathbb{R}, 
T_\rho \mathcal{P}(X)
= \{ \nabla \psi : \psi \in \mathbb{R}^X \},
\quad
(\nabla \psi)(x,y) = \psi(x) - \psi(y),
 and the Riemannian inner product between two tangent vectors \nabla \varphi and \nabla \psi is 
\langle \nabla \varphi, \nabla \psi \rangle_\rho
=
\frac{1}{2} \sum_{x,y \in X}
(\varphi(x) - \varphi(y))(\psi(x) - \psi(y))
\, K(x,y)\, \rho(x,y)\, \pi(x).

This induces a genuine Riemannian metric, and the geodesic distance associated with it is precisely W(\rho^0, \rho^1).
Gradient Flow of the Entropy
Under this metric, the Markov semigroup (P_t)_{t \ge 0} generated by K is the Wasserstein gradient flow of the entropy functional \mathcal{H}.
That is, 
\frac{d}{dt}\rho_t = -\mathrm{grad}_W\, \mathcal{H}(\rho_t),
 and the explicit evolution is the discrete heat equation: 
\frac{d}{dt}\rho_t(x)
= \sum_{y \in X} K(x,y) \big(\log \rho_t(y) - \log \rho_t(x)\big).

Intuition

The logarithmic mean \theta plays the role of an interpolation between densities at neighbouring nodes, analogous to how \rho(x)\nabla\psi(x) represents mass flux in the continuum.
The metric W behaves like the L^2-Wasserstein distance but is adapted to the topology and transition structure of the Markov chain.
The resulting geometry turns \mathcal{P}(X) into a Riemannian manifold, often referred to as the Maas–Mielke–Erbar discrete Wasserstein manifold.

title: Generalising Kernelised Gradient Flows
text:
Dirichlet‐form view: continuum ↔︎ discrete
0) Data

Continuum: domain \Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d, background metric Euclidean, reference law \pi(dx)=e^{-V(x)}dx (reversible for Langevin).
Discrete: finite state space X, reversible kernel K(x,y) with stationary law \pi: 
\pi(x)K(x,y)=\pi(y)K(y,x).


1) Generator and Dirichlet form
Continuum - Generator (symmetric in L^2(\pi)): 
  L f = \Delta f - \nabla V\!\cdot\!\nabla f.
   - Dirichlet form (carré du champ \Gamma): 
  \mathcal{E}(f,g)=\int \nabla f\cdot \nabla g\, d\pi,
  \qquad \Gamma(f)=|\nabla f|^2.
  
Discrete - Generator (on functions f:X\to\mathbb{R}): 
  L f(x)=\sum_{y}K(x,y)\,\big(f(y)-f(x)\big).
   - Dirichlet form and discrete \Gamma: 
  \mathcal{E}(f,g)=\tfrac12\sum_{x,y}\big(f(y)-f(x)\big)\big(g(y)-g(x)\big)\,K(x,y)\,\pi(x),
   
  \Gamma(f)(x)=\tfrac12\sum_{y}\big(f(y)-f(x)\big)^2 K(x,y).
  
These encode the dissipation intrinsic to the dynamics (diffusion vs. jumps).
2) Onsager operator and Riemannian metric tensor
Continuum (Otto calculus) - Identify a tangent vector at \rho by a potential \psi via the continuity equation: 
  \partial_t \rho + \nabla\!\cdot(\rho \nabla \psi)=0.
   - Onsager operator K_\rho (maps potentials to density–velocities): 
  K_\rho \psi = -\,\nabla\!\cdot(\rho \nabla \psi).
   - Metric tensor at \rho: 
  \langle \nabla\varphi,\nabla\psi\rangle_\rho
  =\int \nabla\varphi\cdot\nabla\psi\,\rho\,dx.
  
Discrete (Maas) - Discrete continuity equation for a curve \rho_t and potential \psi_t: 
  \frac{d}{dt}\rho_t(x)
  +\sum_{y}\big(\psi_t(y)-\psi_t(x)\big)K(x,y)\,\theta\!\big(\rho_t(x),\rho_t(y)\big)=0.
   - Edge‐interpolation (logarithmic mean): 
  \theta(s,t)=\frac{s-t}{\log s-\log t},\quad \text{symm., positive}.
   - Onsager operator K_\rho (discrete): 
  (K_\rho \psi)(x)
  =-\sum_{y}\big(\psi(y)-\psi(x)\big)\,K(x,y)\,\theta\!\big(\rho(x),\rho(y)\big).
   - Metric tensor at \rho: 
  \langle \nabla\varphi,\nabla\psi\rangle_\rho
  =\tfrac12\sum_{x,y}\big(\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)\big)\big(\psi(x)-\psi(y)\big)\,
  K(x,y)\,\theta\!\big(\rho(x),\rho(y)\big)\,\pi(x).
  

Heuristics: the continuum weight \rho(x) on fluxes is replaced by an edge weight \theta(\rho(x),\rho(y)) that is the correct discrete analogue for entropy dissipation.

3) Gradient flow of entropy
Functional in both cases: relative entropy w.r.t. \pi 
\mathcal{H}(\rho)=\int \rho\log\frac{\rho}{\pi}\,dx
\;\;\;\text{(continuum)},\qquad
\mathcal{H}(\rho)=\sum_x \pi(x)\rho(x)\log\rho(x)
\;\;\;\text{(discrete)}.

Steepest descent: \partial_t \rho_t=-K_{\rho_t}\big(\delta\mathcal{H}/\delta\rho_t\big).

Continuum: \delta\mathcal{H}/\delta\rho=\log\rho+\text{const} gives 
\partial_t \rho_t
=\nabla\!\cdot\big(\rho_t \nabla \log \rho_t\big)
=\Delta \rho_t \quad (\text{w.r.t. }dx),
 or with \pi\propto e^{-V}, 
\partial_t \rho_t=\nabla\!\cdot\!\big(\rho_t\nabla(\log \rho_t+V)\big)
=\Delta \rho_t+\nabla\!\cdot(\rho_t\nabla V),
 i.e. Fokker–Planck/heat as W_2–gradient flow of entropy.
Discrete (with logarithmic mean): 
\partial_t \rho_t(x)
=\sum_{y}K(x,y)\,\theta\!\big(\rho_t(x),\rho_t(y)\big)\,\big(\log \rho_t(y)-\log \rho_t(x)\big),
 which is exactly the Markov heat flow (the symmetric gradient flow of \mathcal{H}).

4) Dynamic (Benamou–Brenier) distances and JKO schemes
Continuum W_2 - Benamou–Brenier: 
  W_2^2(\rho^0,\rho^1)=\inf_{\rho_t,v_t}\int_0^1\!\!\int |v_t|^2\,\rho_t\,dx\,dt
  \;\;\text{s.t.}\;\;
  \partial_t\rho_t+\nabla\!\cdot(\rho_t v_t)=0.
   - JKO (minimising movement): 
  \rho^{k+1}\in\arg\min_\rho\Big\{\mathcal{H}(\rho)+\tfrac{1}{2\tau}W_2^2(\rho,\rho^k)\Big\}.
  
Discrete (Maas distance W) - Discrete Benamou–Brenier: 
  W(\rho^0,\rho^1)^2
  =\inf_{\rho_t,\psi_t}\int_0^1 \tfrac12\sum_{x,y}\big(\psi_t(x)-\psi_t(y)\big)^2
  K(x,y)\,\theta(\rho_t(x),\rho_t(y))\,\pi(x)\,dt
   s.t. the discrete continuity equation. - Discrete JKO: 
  \rho^{k+1}\in\arg\min_\rho\Big\{\mathcal{H}(\rho)+\tfrac{1}{2\tau}W(\rho,\rho^k)^2\Big\},
   and as \tau\downarrow0 this time–steps the Markov semigroup.
5) Diffusive limit: how the discrete recovers the continuum
Consider a random walk on the lattice h\mathbb{Z}^d with jump rates K_h(x,x\pm h e_i)\sim h^{-2} (reversible w.r.t. uniform \pi_h).
As h\to0: - The generator L_h converges to the Laplacian (or to \Delta-\nabla V\cdot\nabla in a weighted setup). - The edge weight \theta\!\big(\rho(x),\rho(y)\big) between nearest neighbours satisfies 
  \theta(\rho(x),\rho(x+h e_i))=\rho(x)+\mathcal{O}(h),
   so the discrete fluxes $ K_h,(),((y)-(x)) $ approximate \rho\,\partial_{e_i}\psi. - The Maas metric W_h \Gamma–converges (in suitable senses) to W_2, and the discrete JKO scheme converges to the continuous JKO for entropy.
Moral: in the continuum you “see” \rho weighting |\nabla\psi|^2; on graphs you must weight edges by \theta(\rho_x,\rho_y) so that, under mesh refinement, this becomes the correct \rho weight.
6) Why the dependence on \pi appears only discretely

Continuum: geometry comes from the base metric; \pi only enters the functional (entropy w.r.t. \pi) or the drift in the generator.
Discrete: geometry must be engineered from the chain; reversibility \pi(x)K(x,y) fixes the symmetric Dirichlet form, and the logarithmic mean aligns dissipation with the entropy’s first variation.

One‐line dictionary

\boxed{
\text{Continuum: } K_\rho \psi = -\nabla\!\cdot(\rho\nabla\psi)
\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{Discrete: } (K_\rho \psi)(x) = -\sum_y (\psi(y)-\psi(x))K(x,y)\,\theta(\rho_x,\rho_y)
}

This is the precise Dirichlet‐form/Onsager correspondence that makes “heat = entropy gradient flow” true on both sides.

title: Generalising Kernelised Gradient Flows
text:
SVGD for general diffusions
From “De-randomizing MCMC dynamics with the diffusion Stein operator”, there is a general correspondence:

\text{Stein Operators} \iff \text{Diffusions} \iff \text{Gradient Flows}

Diffusions
The general form of an Ito diffusion with stationary distribution \pi is

dX_t = f() dt + (A + C) dW_t.

This defines both a generator and a Fokker-Planck equation:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{J}f &= ... \\
\partial_t q &= \mathcal{J}^* q.
\end{align*}
Gradient Flow
It was shown that the Fokker-Planck can always be written as a “gradient flow” with respect to the KLD:

\partial_t q = -\nabla\cdot(q (A+C) \nabla \frac{\delta \mathrm{KLD}(q\|\pi)}{\delta q}).

Here:

A defines a intrinsic metric on \mathbb{R}^d, which adjusts the Wasserstein metric accordingly 
W_2(P,Q) = \inf_{\gamma \in \Gamma(P,Q)} \left(\int \|x - y\|_A^2 \,\mathrm{d}\gamma(x,y) \right)^{1/2}

C defines a symplectic form (Hamiltonian part) giving the manifold symplectic structure as well. (Flows have rotations around level sets.)

Stein Operators
The generator defines a Stein operator over test functions:

\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{J} f] = 0.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
Which answer is better?

Prompt:
“In at most two sentences, explain the offside rule to a 10-year-old.”




Answer A
In football, you’re offside if your teammate passes the ball to you while you are nearer to the other team’s goal than both the ball and the second-last defender. But it only matters if you are involved in the play, like trying to get the ball or blocking an opponent.



Answer B
To stay “onside,” you must have at least two opponents (usually the goalie and one defender) between you and the goal line at the moment the ball is kicked to you. Basically, you can’t “cherry-pick” by hanging out behind the last defender to wait for an easy pass!



Answer C
The offside rule means you can’t hang out too close to the other team’s goal waiting for the ball—you need to have at least two players from the other team (usually the goalkeeper and one defender) between you and their goal line when the ball is passed to you. It’s there to keep the game fair and make sure players have to work together to move the ball forward instead of just camping by the goal!



Question: Which answer would you prefer: A, B, or C?


RLHF starts from data like this:
humans compare model outputs, and we fit a scoring model that predicts which response people prefer.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
What is an LLM?

A large language model is typically a causal decoder-only transformer, trained to predict the next token from the previous tokens.

Given text

x_1, x_2, \dots, x_t,

the model estimates

p_\theta(x_{t+1} \mid x_1,\dots,x_t).


For example, after

The striker was clearly in an offside…

the model assigns probabilities to possible next tokens:

\text{position},\quad \text{trap},\quad \text{decision},\quad \ldots



Pretraining teaches the model to be a text continuation engine.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
How is it trained?


Text data


→


Next-token prediction


→


Base LLM


The pretraining loss is the negative log-likelihood:

\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\sum_t \log p_\theta(x_{t+1} \mid x_1,\dots,x_t).


This objective is not

“be helpful”
“be truthful”
“follow instructions”
“give the answer humans prefer”



A base LLM is cool, but merely text continuation isn’t enough for many applications: we want to align the model with human preferences

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
section: Why next-token prediction is not enough
text:
Why next-token prediction is not enough



Pretraining objective
Predict the next token:

\mathcal{L}(\theta)
=
-\sum_t
\log p_\theta(x_{t+1}\mid x_1,\dots,x_t).


This rewards outputs that are likely under the training data.




Assistant objective
Produce responses humans judge as:

helpful and clear
truthful
safe
appropriate to the user’s intent


This rewards outputs that are preferred by people.




The core mismatch:

\text{likely text} \neq \text{desirable answer}.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
The RLHF pipeline



1


Supervised fine-tuning
Prompt \to human-written good answer
Gives an SFT model.




2


Train a reward/scoring model
Humans compare model outputs.
Gives a learned score r_\phi(x,y).




3


Optimise the LLM against the learned score
The language model is fine-tuned to produce high-scoring answers.




RLHF turns human preference judgements into a training signal for the language model.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
Stage 1: Supervised fine-tuning



Training data
Human-written demonstrations:

(x_i, y_i^{\mathrm{demo}})

where

x_i is a prompt
y_i^{\mathrm{demo}} is a good assistant answer




Objective
Fine-tune the model to imitate good answers:

\max_\theta
\sum_i
\log \pi_\theta
\left(
y_i^{\mathrm{demo}} \mid x_i
\right).

This gives the SFT model.



SFT teaches the model the format of helpful assistant behaviour.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
What is \pi_\theta(y \mid x)?



Transformer model
The transformer takes a sequence of tokens and outputs next-token probabilities:

p_\theta(x_{t+1} \mid x_{\leq t}).

The parameters \theta are the neural-network weights:

attention weights
feedforward weights
embedding matrices
output projection




Policy notation
For a prompt x, the model generates an answer y token by token:

y = (y_1,\dots,y_T).

So we can write the probability of the whole answer as

\pi_\theta(y \mid x)
=
\prod_{t=1}^{T}
p_\theta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t}).




\pi_\theta is not a separate model.
It is the same transformer, viewed as a probability distribution over generated answers.


This is an important notational point.
In language modelling, we usually write the model as next-token probabilities.
In reinforcement learning, we often call the model a policy because it chooses actions. Here, the “actions” are tokens, or equivalently the generated answer.
So: - the transformer is the architecture; - \theta are the weights; - p_\theta is the next-token distribution; - \pi_\theta(y \mid x) is the induced distribution over full answers.
This lets us use reinforcement-learning language later, where the language model is the policy and the generated response is the action or trajectory.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
SFT as next-token training
A human demonstration is a prompt-answer pair:

(x_i, y_i^{\mathrm{demo}}).

If

y_i^{\mathrm{demo}}
=
(y_{i1},\dots,y_{iT_i}),

then the model assigns probability

\pi_\theta(y_i^{\mathrm{demo}} \mid x_i)
=
\prod_{t=1}^{T_i}
p_\theta(y_{it} \mid x_i, y_{i,<t}).

Therefore SFT maximises

\sum_i \log \pi_\theta(y_i^{\mathrm{demo}} \mid x_i)
=
\sum_i \sum_{t=1}^{T_i}
\log p_\theta(y_{it} \mid x_i, y_{i,<t}).


SFT is ordinary next-token training, but on curated prompt-answer examples.


This slide clarifies that SFT is not a fundamentally different training method from pretraining.
It is still next-token prediction.
The difference is the dataset: - pretraining uses broad internet-scale text; - SFT uses curated demonstrations of good assistant behaviour.
So SFT shifts the model from “continue arbitrary text” towards “respond to instructions in an assistant-like way”.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
Stage 2: Train a scoring model
For a prompt x, sample two candidate answers:

y_A, \; y_B \sim \pi_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\cdot \mid x).

A human is asked:

Which answer is better?

y_A \succ y_B
\qquad \text{or} \qquad
y_B \succ y_A


The reward model is a scoring function:

r_\phi(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}.


The statistical problem is to infer latent answer quality from noisy pairwise comparisons.


This is the point that connects most directly to the sports research group.
The reward model does not observe true answer quality. It only observes comparative human judgements.
So this is a paired-comparison problem: answer A beats answer B, or answer B beats answer A.
The word “reward model” is common in RLHF, but for this talk it is useful to call it a scoring model.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
The preference model
A standard model is logistic:

\Pr(y_A \succ y_B \mid x)
=
\sigma
\left(
r_\phi(x,y_A) - r_\phi(x,y_B)
\right),

where

\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-z)}.


This is like saying:

Answer A “beats” answer B with probability determined by the difference in their latent scores.



This is essentially the Bradley-Terry model from paired-comparison statistics.


This is the main scoring-model slide.
Make the sports analogy explicit: in sport, we often infer latent team or player quality from match outcomes. In RLHF, we infer latent answer quality from human preference outcomes.
The model says that only the difference in scores matters: if answer A has a much higher score than answer B, humans are very likely to prefer A. If their scores are close, the preference is uncertain.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
section: How is the scoring model trained?
text:
How is the scoring model trained?



Typical architecture
Given a prompt-answer pair (x,y), concatenate the tokens and feed them through a transformer:

[x \, ; \, y]
\;\longrightarrow\;
h_1,\dots,h_T

Use the final hidden representation (or EOS-token representation) and attach a scalar head:

r_\phi(x,y) = w^\top h_T + b.

So the reward model is typically:

a transformer backbone
plus a 1-dimensional linear “score head”
outputting a single real number




Training from preferences
Training data consist of triples

(x_i, y_i^+, y_i^-),

where y_i^+ is the human-preferred answer and y_i^- is the rejected one.
The same scorer is applied to both answers, and we minimise

\mathcal{L}(\phi)
=
-
\sum_i
\log
\sigma\!\left(
r_\phi(x_i,y_i^+) - r_\phi(x_i,y_i^-)
\right).

This pushes the preferred answer to have the higher score.



Architecturally, the scoring model is usually just another language model with a scalar scoring head.


Statistically, this is just a paired-comparison model fit by logistic loss.


This slide is meant to demystify the reward model.
The input is not “answer A versus answer B” jointly. Rather, the same scoring model is applied separately to each prompt-answer pair: - score prompt + answer A - score prompt + answer B
Then the difference of the two scores is passed through a logistic function, giving the model probability that A is preferred to B.
In practice, the reward model is often initialised from a pretrained or SFT transformer, then fitted with this pairwise preference loss.
So: - the transformer provides contextual representations; - the scalar head converts the representation into a latent quality score; - the logistic loss learns from human comparisons.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
section: Scoring model as a comparison machine
text:
Scoring model as a comparison machine


Prompt x + Answer y_A


→


Score 
r_\phi(x,y_A)






Prompt x + Answer y_B


→


Score 
r_\phi(x,y_B)




\Pr(y_A \succ y_B \mid x)
=
\sigma\!\left(
r_\phi(x,y_A)-r_\phi(x,y_B)
\right).


Score each answer separately, then compare the scores.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
Stage 3: Optimise the LLM
Now treat the language model as a policy:

\pi_\theta(y \mid x),

where

x is the prompt
y is the generated answer

The objective is:

\max_\theta
\;
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)}
\left[
r_\phi(x,y)
-
\beta
\operatorname{KL}
\left(
\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)
\Vert
\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)
\right)
\right].


The reward model is the judge.
The language model is the competitor.


RLHF trains the competitor to get higher marks from the judge, without drifting too far from the original model.


Historically, this optimisation was often done with PPO.
The KL penalty is important: without it, the model may exploit weaknesses in the reward model. The reference model is usually the SFT model or another earlier checkpoint.
The intuition: - the reward term says “produce answers humans would prefer”; - the KL term says “do not move too far from the model we already trust”.
This is the bridge into policy optimisation.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
Text generation as reinforcement learning



Language modelling view
Given a prompt x, the model generates an answer token by token:

y = (y_1,\dots,y_T).

The transformer defines

\pi_\theta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t}).

The probability of the full answer is

\pi_\theta(y \mid x)
=
\prod_{t=1}^T
\pi_\theta(y_t \mid x,y_{<t}).




Reinforcement learning view
The language model is a policy.
At step t:

state: current text context (x,y_{<t})
action: next token y_t
trajectory: full answer y
reward: score from reward model


R(x,y) = r_\phi(x,y).




In RLHF, generating an answer is treated as a sequential decision problem.


This slide maps language modelling onto reinforcement learning.
The policy is not a separate object. It is the same transformer model, but interpreted as a policy over tokens.
The state is the current text context. The action is the next token. The trajectory is the complete generated response.
The reward is usually only given after the whole answer has been generated, because the reward model scores the complete prompt-answer pair.
This is why the setting is naturally an episodic reinforcement-learning problem: one prompt gives one generated answer, and the answer receives a scalar reward.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
The RLHF objective
For prompts x \sim \mathcal{D}, generate answers

y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x).

The aim is to maximise expected reward:

\max_\theta
\;
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D}}
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)}
\left[
r_\phi(x,y)
\right].


But if we optimise only this reward, the model may exploit weaknesses in the reward model.


So we add a penalty for moving too far from a reference model.


\max_\theta
\;
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D}}
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)}
\left[
r_\phi(x,y)
-
\beta
\operatorname{KL}
\left(
\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)
\Vert
\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)
\right)
\right].


This is the cleaner version of the objective.
The previous slide only wrote the expectation over y, but really there is also an expectation over prompts x drawn from some prompt distribution.
The reference model is usually the supervised fine-tuned model, or a frozen copy of a previous model.
The KL penalty discourages the model from drifting too far away from the model we already trust. This matters because the reward model is imperfect. If the policy is allowed to optimise the reward model too aggressively, it can discover unnatural answers that get high reward-model scores but are bad for humans.
This is analogous to regularisation.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
Why only approximately?
The objective is:

\mathbb{E}
\left[
r_\phi(x,y)
-
\beta
\operatorname{KL}
\left(
\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)
\Vert
\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)
\right)
\right].

In practice, this is optimised approximately using samples.



What we can sample
We sample prompts:

x_i \sim \mathcal{D}.

Then sample model answers:

y_i \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x_i).

Then score them:

r_\phi(x_i,y_i).




What we approximate
The expectation is approximated by minibatches.
The KL term is usually estimated token by token.
The policy update is done using a stable policy-gradient method, often PPO.



“Approximate” means: sample-based optimisation of a regularised expected reward objective.


This slide explains the word approximate.
There are several approximations: 1. We use samples of prompts, not the full prompt distribution. 2. We use sampled model completions, not all possible completions. 3. The KL penalty is estimated using token probabilities from the current model and reference model. 4. The policy-gradient update uses a practical surrogate objective, such as PPO, rather than exactly maximising the displayed expression.
So the displayed equation is the conceptual objective. PPO is one practical method for taking stable gradient steps towards improving that objective.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
section: Why is there a KL penalty?
text:
Why is there a KL penalty?
In principle, we could optimise only the reward model:

\max_\theta
\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}
[
r_\phi(x,y)
].

But the reward model is only a learned proxy for human preference.
So RLHF usually solves a regularised problem:

\max_\theta
\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}
\left[
r_\phi(x,y)
-
\beta
\log
\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}
{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)}
\right].


The KL penalty says: improve according to the reward model, but stay close to the reference model.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
Policy-gradient intuition
Suppose the model samples an answer

y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x).

If the answer receives high reward, we want to make it more likely.
If it receives low reward, we want to make it less likely.
A basic policy-gradient update has the form

\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
\approx
\left(
R(x,y) - b(x)
\right)
\nabla_\theta
\log \pi_\theta(y \mid x),

where

R(x,y)
=
r_\phi(x,y)
-
\beta
\operatorname{KL}
\left(
\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)
\Vert
\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)
\right).


Reward-weighted maximum likelihood: make high-scoring sampled answers more likely.


This is not the exact PPO objective, but it gives the core intuition.
The term \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x) tells us how to change the model parameters to increase the probability of the sampled answer.
The scalar reward term tells us whether that sampled answer should be encouraged or discouraged.
The baseline b(x) reduces variance. In actor-critic methods, this baseline is learned by a value function.
PPO modifies this basic idea by restricting how large the policy update can be. This makes training more stable.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
Why PPO?
A naive policy-gradient update can change the model too aggressively.
PPO uses a clipped objective that discourages overly large policy updates.
Define the probability ratio

\rho_t(\theta)
=
\frac{
\pi_\theta(y_t \mid x,y_{<t})
}{
\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_t \mid x,y_{<t})
}.

PPO encourages high-reward tokens while keeping

\rho_t(\theta)

close to 1.

PPO is a practical stabilisation method: improve the policy, but do not let it move too far in one update.


You probably do not need to derive PPO fully.
The key idea is that PPO compares the new policy to the old policy. If the new policy makes a token much more or less likely than before, the clipped objective limits the update.
This sits alongside the KL penalty to the reference model: - PPO controls step size relative to the previous model; - the KL penalty controls drift relative to the trusted reference model.
For this talk, the important point is not PPO itself. The important point is that the LLM is being updated using policy-gradient style reinforcement learning, with the learned reward model providing the reward signal.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
The scoring-model perspective

From a statistical perspective, the exciting object is not really
reinforcement learning.
It is the learned scoring model.


RLHF turns qualitative human judgements into a quantitative objective.



Human comparisons


→


Latent score model


→


Optimisation target

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
section: From Elo-style scores to RLHF scores
text:
From Elo-style scores to RLHF scores



Sport / Elo setting
A competitor has a persistent latent score:

s_i \in \mathbb{R}.

For two competitors,

\mathbb{P}(i \succ j)
=
\sigma(s_i - s_j).


The same competitors appear repeatedly.




RLHF setting
A prompt–answer pair has a latent score:

r_\phi(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}.

For two answers to the same prompt,

\mathbb{P}(y_A \succ y_B \mid x)
=
\sigma\{r_\phi(x,y_A)-r_\phi(x,y_B)\}.


The same exact answer to the same exact prompt may never appear again.




Ranking systems typically score persistent competitors; RLHF scores context-dependent outputs.


This slide makes the mapping to sports statistics explicit.
In a simple Elo or Bradley–Terry setting, each team or player has a latent score. The same teams appear repeatedly, so it is plausible to maintain a table of scores and update them over time.
In RLHF, the object being scored is not just “the model” globally. The reward model scores a particular answer in response to a particular prompt. That is a much higher-dimensional object.
So the score cannot usually be a simple parameter s_i attached to a named competitor. Instead, we need a function approximator r_\phi(x,y) which can generalise across prompts and answers.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
section: Why use a scoring model at all?
text:
Why use a scoring model at all?
If every prompt–answer pair had its own unrelated score, we would need something like

s_{x,y}.

But this is impossible in practice.



Sports ratings
A small set of recurring objects:

\text{Team A}, \text{Team B}, \text{Team C}, \ldots


Many repeated observations per competitor.


A table of scores is plausible: 
s_1,\ldots,s_N.





LLM outputs
A huge space of possible objects:

(x,y) \in \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}.


Most prompt–answer pairs are observed rarely or never.


We need a learned function: 
r_\phi : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \to \mathbb{R}.





The reward model is a generalising scoring rule, not just a table of ratings.


This is the key statistical reason for using a neural reward model.
In Elo, the score belongs to a persistent competitor. A team plays many matches, so we can update its rating.
In RLHF, each output is more like a one-off performance in a high-dimensional context. The exact prompt and exact answer may never recur. Therefore we cannot assign an independent parameter to every possible pair (x,y).
Instead, we train a model r_\phi(x,y) that learns features of good answers: relevance, clarity, correctness, helpfulness, style, safety, and so on. It must generalise from observed comparisons to new prompts and new answers.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
section: The scoring model is trained from comparisons
text:
The scoring model is trained from comparisons
For a prompt x, suppose a human prefers answer y_A to answer y_B:

y_A \succ y_B.

The scoring model should assign the preferred answer a higher score:

r_\phi(x,y_A) > r_\phi(x,y_B).

A Bradley–Terry-style likelihood writes this as

\mathbb{P}(y_A \succ y_B \mid x)
=
\sigma\{r_\phi(x,y_A)-r_\phi(x,y_B)\}.


The model learns a scoring function by being punished when its score differences disagree with human preferences.


This slide returns from the sports analogy to the RLHF training objective.
The key idea is simple: if humans prefer y_A to y_B, then the reward model should give y_A a higher score.
The Bradley–Terry likelihood turns this into a differentiable loss. Other scoring models would change the likelihood, but the basic idea remains: learn scores whose implied preferences match human judgements.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
Stage 2 observes judgements, not scores
For a prompt x, suppose the model produces candidate answers

y_1,\ldots,y_K.

A human annotator does not provide the true rewards

r_\phi(x,y_1),\ldots,r_\phi(x,y_K).

Instead, they provide an observation:


y_A \succ y_B


y_A \sim y_B


y_1 \succ y_3 \succ y_2


\text{``answer } y_A \text{ is 4/5''}



The reward model is trained by choosing a likelihood for the kind of judgement we observe.


This is the transition from the intuitive point that pairwise comparisons are easier to the statistical point that different data types require different observation models.
The human does not reveal the reward function. They provide noisy evidence about it.
So the role of Stage 2 is to infer a scoring function from whatever kind of judgement data we collect: pairwise preferences, ties, rankings, ratings, or something else.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
Same scoring function, different likelihood
The scoring model is still a function

r_\phi : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \to \mathbb{R}.

What changes is the probability model for the observed judgement:

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RM}}(\phi)
=
-
\log p_\phi
\left(
\text{human judgement}
\mid
x,y_1,\ldots,y_K
\right).




Examples of observations
Pairwise preference:

y_A \succ y_B

Tie or no preference:

y_A \sim y_B

Ranking:

y_1 \succ y_2 \succ y_3




Examples of likelihoods
Bradley–Terry
Davidson / tie models
Plackett–Luce
Ordinal rating models



Different judgement data change the Stage 2 loss, not the basic idea of learning a scalar reward.


This is the main statistical message.
The scoring model produces a scalar score for each prompt-answer pair. But we never directly observe that scalar score.
Instead, we specify a likelihood connecting the scores to the human judgement. If the judgement is pairwise, we might use Bradley–Terry. If ties are allowed, we use a tie model. If the annotator ranks several answers, we might use Plackett–Luce.
The final Stage 3 RLHF step only needs the trained scalar reward model r_\phi(x,y).

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
section: Pairwise comparison is easier than absolute scoring
text:
Pairwise comparison is easier than absolute scoring



Absolute scoring
Hard for humans:

\text{This answer is } 7.3/10.


What exactly does 7.3 mean?




Pairwise comparison
Usually easier:

y_A \succ y_B.


This answer is better than that one.




This is why paired-comparison models are attractive in sport, rankings, judging, and psychometrics.


Make the point intuitively.
Humans are often bad at calibrated absolute scoring, but much better at relative judgements.
This is one reason RLHF usually uses comparisons rather than asking annotators to give precise numerical scores.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
Bradley–Terry: the simplest paired-comparison model
Suppose item i has latent score s_i and item j has latent score s_j.
A Bradley–Terry model says

\mathbb{P}(i \succ j)
=
\frac{\exp(s_i)}{\exp(s_i) + \exp(s_j)}
=
\sigma(s_i - s_j).




Sport

\mathbb{P}(\text{Team A beats Team B})
=
\sigma(s_A - s_B).




RLHF

\mathbb{P}(y_A \succ y_B \mid x)
=
\sigma(r_\phi(x,y_A) - r_\phi(x,y_B)).




Only the difference in scores matters.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
What about draws?
Bradley–Terry only allows

i \succ j
\qquad \text{or} \qquad
j \succ i.

What about draws?



Sport
Football matches etc. can end in a draw:

i \sim j.




RLHF
Two answers may be equally good, equally bad, or too close to call:

y_A \sim y_B.




One extension is the Davidson model:

\mathbb{P}(i \succ j)
=
\frac{\alpha_i}{\alpha_i + \alpha_j + \nu \sqrt{\alpha_i\alpha_j}},


\mathbb{P}(i \sim j)
=
\frac{\nu \sqrt{\alpha_i\alpha_j}}{\alpha_i + \alpha_j + \nu \sqrt{\alpha_i\alpha_j}},

where \alpha_i = \exp(s_i) and \nu \geq 0 controls the tendency for draws.


This is a good example because it connects naturally to sport.
The ordinary Bradley–Terry model forces every comparison to have a winner. But in football, chess, judged sport, and human preference annotation, sometimes the honest answer is: these are about the same.
The draw parameter \nu controls how much probability is given to ties. If \nu=0, we recover the no-draw version.
For RLHF, this matters because forcing annotators to choose a winner between two nearly identical answers can add noise.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
What about rankings?
In principle, a human annotator can rank several options:

i_1 \succ i_2 \succ \cdots \succ i_K.

A common model is the Plackett–Luce model:

\mathbb{P}(i_1 \succ i_2 \succ \cdots \succ i_K)
=
\prod_{m=1}^{K}
\frac{\exp(s_{i_m})}
{\sum_{\ell=m}^{K} \exp(s_{i_\ell})}.




Sport
Rank players, teams, performances, or candidates:

\text{Gold} \succ \text{Silver} \succ \text{Bronze}.




RLHF
Rank several candidate answers to the same prompt:

y_1 \succ y_3 \succ y_2 \succ y_4.




This slide shows that pairwise comparisons are not the only possible data format.
Instead of asking a human to compare two answers, we might ask them to rank four answers. This gives richer information, but it may also be harder for the human annotator.
The Plackett–Luce model says: first choose the best item from the full set, then choose the best item from the remaining set, and so on.
Again, the same latent-score idea appears.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
section: The RLHF version: scores depend on context
text:
The RLHF version: scores depend on context
In most ranking systems we have a fixed score for each competitor:

s_i.

But in RLHF, the score depends on both the prompt and the answer:

r_\phi(x,y).




Fixed ability
A team-strength model might say:

s_i = \text{ability of team } i.

The score belongs mainly to the team.



Context-dependent quality
An answer-quality model says:

r_\phi(x,y) = \text{quality of answer } y \text{ for prompt } x.

The score belongs to the pair (x,y).



The same answer can be excellent for one prompt and terrible for another.


This is an important conceptual move.
In a basic Bradley–Terry model, each object has a fixed latent score. But in RLHF the score is context-dependent. The reward model is not asking whether an answer is globally good. It is asking whether this answer is good for this prompt.
This is also familiar in sport. A tactical decision may be good in one match state and bad in another. A player action may be good depending on scoreline, opponent, weather, time remaining, formation, and so on.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
section: What changes if we change the scoring model?
text:
What changes if we change the scoring model?
The RLHF pipeline stays mostly the same:

\text{human judgements}
\to
\text{reward model}
\to
\text{policy optimisation}.

Changing the scoring model mainly changes the reward-model loss:

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RM}}(\phi)
=
-\log p_\phi(\text{judgement} \mid x, y_1,\ldots,y_K).

Bradley–Terry, Plackett–Luce, tie models, and ordinal models give different likelihoods.

But Stage 3 only sees the resulting scalar reward 
r_\phi(x,y).

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
A variant: Direct Preference Optimisation
Classical RLHF separates two steps:


Stage 2: Train reward model


→


Stage 3: Optimise policy with RL


DPO collapses these into one preference-learning objective.
Given preference data of pairwise comparisons

(x, y_w, y_l),

DPO directly fine-tunes the language model so that the preferred answer becomes more likely than the rejected answer:

\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)
\quad \text{increases relative to} \quad
\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x).


The reward model r_\phi(x,y) has not disappeared completely. Instead, it is implicit in the policy update.


DPO stands for Direct Preference Optimisation.
It is often described as RLHF without reinforcement learning, because it avoids a separate reward model and PPO-style policy optimisation.
However, conceptually it is still doing preference-based alignment. It uses the same kind of human comparison data, but turns it directly into a loss for the language model.
The reference model, usually the SFT model, prevents the new model from moving too far away from the original assistant model.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
section: Classical RLHF has two mathematical steps
text:
Classical RLHF has two mathematical steps
Classical RLHF separates the problem into two stages.



Stage 2: fit a reward model
Given preference data

(x,y_w,y_l),

train r_\phi(x,y) so that

r_\phi(x,y_w) > r_\phi(x,y_l).

For Bradley–Terry:

\mathbb{P}_\phi(y_w \succ y_l \mid x)
=
\sigma
\left(
r_\phi(x,y_w)-r_\phi(x,y_l)
\right).




Stage 3: optimise the policy
Then fine-tune the language model

\pi_\theta(y \mid x)

to maximise reward while staying close to a reference model:

\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x).




DPO starts by asking whether these two steps can be algebraically collapsed.


Here y_w means the winning or preferred answer, and y_l means the losing or rejected answer.
In the classical pipeline, the reward model is trained first. Then it is frozen and used as the reward signal for policy optimisation.
DPO asks: if we know the form of the preference likelihood and the form of the policy optimisation problem, can we remove the explicit reward model?

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
Stage 3: KL-regularised reward maximisation
For a fixed prompt x, classical RLHF approximately solves

\max_{\pi}
\;
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi(\cdot \mid x)}
\left[
r(x,y)
\right]
-
\beta
\operatorname{KL}
\left(
\pi(\cdot \mid x)
\Vert
\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)
\right).

Equivalently,

\max_{\pi}
\sum_y \pi(y \mid x) r(x,y)
-
\beta
\sum_y
\pi(y \mid x)
\log
\frac{\pi(y \mid x)}
{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}.


The reward encourages preferred outputs; the KL penalty stops the model drifting too far from the reference model.


This is the usual RLHF objective in simplified form.
The policy \pi is the language model being fine-tuned. The reference policy \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is usually the supervised fine-tuned model.
The constant \beta > 0 controls the reward–KL trade-off. Smaller \beta means the model is allowed to move more aggressively towards high-reward answers. Larger \beta keeps it closer to the reference model.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
section: The optimal policy has a closed form
text:
The optimal policy has a closed form
For a fixed reward function r(x,y), the solution has the form

\pi_r(y \mid x)
=
\frac{1}{Z_r(x)}
\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)
\exp
\left(
\frac{1}{\beta} r(x,y)
\right),

where

Z_r(x)
=
\sum_y
\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)
\exp
\left(
\frac{1}{\beta} r(x,y)
\right)

is a normalising constant.

High-reward outputs become more likely, but only relative to the reference model.


This is the key mathematical fact behind DPO.
The optimal policy is a tilted version of the reference policy. Outputs with larger reward receive larger probability under the new policy.
The normalising constant Z_r(x) makes the probabilities sum to one.
You do not need to derive this fully in the talk, but it follows from optimising the KL-regularised objective over the probability simplex.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
section: The policy secretly defines a reward model
text:
The policy secretly defines a reward model
Rearranging the closed-form solution gives

r(x,y)
=
\beta
\log
\frac{\pi_r(y \mid x)}
{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}
+
\beta \log Z_r(x).

So, up to a prompt-dependent constant,

r(x,y)
\equiv
\beta
\log
\frac{\pi_r(y \mid x)}
{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}.


A policy can be interpreted as an implicit reward model.


This is the key DPO insight.
If a policy assigns an answer much higher probability than the reference model does, then that answer has high implicit reward.
The term \beta \log Z_r(x) depends only on the prompt x, not on the answer y. Therefore it cancels when comparing two answers to the same prompt.
That cancellation is what lets us substitute this expression directly into the Bradley–Terry preference likelihood.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
Reward differences become log-probability ratios
For two answers y_w and y_l to the same prompt x,

r(x,y_w)-r(x,y_l)
=
\beta
\log
\frac{\pi_r(y_w \mid x)}
{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w \mid x)}
-
\beta
\log
\frac{\pi_r(y_l \mid x)}
{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l \mid x)}.

Equivalently,

r(x,y_w)-r(x,y_l)
=
\beta
\log
\frac{
\pi_r(y_w \mid x)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l \mid x)
}{
\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w \mid x)\pi_r(y_l \mid x)
}.


Preference depends on how much the new policy favours the winner over the loser, relative to the reference model.


This is the bridge from reward modelling to direct policy optimisation.
The reward difference is not just about whether \pi_r(y_w \mid x) is large. It is about whether the policy increases the probability of the preferred answer relative to the reference model, compared with the rejected answer.
That relative-to-reference structure is very important. It prevents the model from simply increasing the probability of generic high-probability text.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
Substitute into the Bradley–Terry likelihood
The Bradley–Terry preference model says

\mathbb{P}(y_w \succ y_l \mid x)
=
\sigma
\left(
r(x,y_w)-r(x,y_l)
\right).

Using the implicit reward expression,

\mathbb{P}_\theta(y_w \succ y_l \mid x)
=
\sigma
\left[
\beta
\log
\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}
{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w \mid x)}
-
\beta
\log
\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}
{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l \mid x)}
\right].


The likelihood is now written directly in terms of the policy \pi_\theta.


This is the algebraic collapse.
In classical RLHF, the Bradley–Terry likelihood is used to train r_\phi.
In DPO, the same Bradley–Terry likelihood is used, but the reward difference is replaced by an expression involving the policy and reference model.
So there is no separate reward-model network. The policy itself defines the implicit reward.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
The DPO loss
DPO minimises the negative log-likelihood of the observed preferences:

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta)
=
-
\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w,y_l)}
\left[
\log
\sigma
\left(
\beta
\log
\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}
{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w \mid x)}
-
\beta
\log
\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}
{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l \mid x)}
\right)
\right].


This is a supervised classification-style loss on preference pairs.


This is the final DPO objective.
The model is rewarded when the preferred answer becomes more likely than the rejected answer relative to the reference model.
Unlike PPO-style RLHF, this does not require sampling new outputs during training, fitting a separate reward model, or running a reinforcement learning algorithm.
However, it still depends on the RLHF objective mathematically: it comes from the closed-form solution of the KL-regularised reward maximisation problem.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
section: The score is latent and context-dependent
text:
The score is latent and context-dependent
The reward model assigns a scalar score:

r_\phi(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}.


But the reward is not a physical quantity.
It is inferred from human preference data.


The same answer may be good in one context and bad in another:

r_\phi(x,y)
\quad \text{depends on both } x \text{ and } y.



Sports analogy
A performance score may depend on:

opposition strength
match context
position or role
tactics
weather
judging criteria



Emphasise that the scoring model is not estimating an intrinsic property of the answer alone.
A response can be excellent for one prompt and terrible for another.
For example, a short answer may be good when the user asks for a quick summary, but bad when they ask for a detailed proof.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
text:
Human preference is noisy
Different humans may disagree.
The same human may be inconsistent.
Some criteria are vague.

So the reward model estimates something like

\Pr(y_A \succ y_B \mid x).



This is not the same as estimating

\text{truth}
\qquad \text{or} \qquad
\text{objective quality}.



The scoring model learns a pattern in human preferences, not a direct measurement of reality.


This is a useful place to be precise.
The target is not “truth” in a philosophical or scientific sense. The data are comparative human judgements.
That can still be very useful, but we should not confuse “preferred by annotators” with “objectively correct”.

title: An Introduction to Scoring Models in RLHF
section: Optimising a learned score can break the score
text:
Optimising a learned score can break the score
Once the model is trained to maximise

r_\phi(x,y),

it may find outputs that get high reward-model scores without genuinely being better.

Goodhart’s law:

When a measure becomes a target, it can stop being a good measure.



Sports analogies

Optimise shots on target
\Rightarrow teams may take many low-quality shots.
Optimise distance covered
\Rightarrow players may run more without playing better.
Optimise a judging rubric
\Rightarrow competitors may learn to game the rubric.



RLHF has the same problem: the model may learn to satisfy the judge rather than genuinely improve.


This is probably the most important warning in the talk.
Say: “The reward model is only a proxy. Once we optimise hard against a proxy, we should expect failure modes.”
In RLHF this is often called reward hacking. The model may discover outputs that exploit weaknesses in the reward model.
This motivates why RLHF systems need careful evaluation, regularisation, human review, and sometimes additional safety constraints.

Move observations toward the origin using a scale r > 0: 
k_r(x,y) = k(rx, ry)
\qquad

g(r),

-

Under what conditions on the kernel k does g'(r) \le 0 hold for all r > 0?

 where \eta is conditionally negative definite (CND).

Theorem 1 (Monotonicity condition) If, for some r>0, the derivative \partial_r \eta_r(x,y) is a CND function, then

=

+

\eta_r'(x_i,x_j)\,
k_r(x_i,x_j)

=
k_r(x_i,0)
-
\lambda \alpha_i

=

\sum_i
\alpha_i^2
\eta_r'(x_i,0)
-
\sum_{i,j}
\alpha_i\alpha_j
\psi_r(x_i,x_j)
k_r(x_i,x_j)

Sign of each term
Since:

\psi_r is PD

both terms are non-positive

A counterexample kernel (Bernstein but not Thorin–Bernstein)
From the Levy–Khintchine representation, take 
f(h)=a+bh+\int_0^\infty (1-e^{-ht})\,\mu(dt),
 and choose a=b=0 and \mu=\delta_1 (Dirac mass at t=1). Then 
f(h)=1-e^{-h}

Therefore the kernel 
k(x,y)=\exp\!\Big\{-f(\|x-y\|^2)\Big\}
=\exp\!\left\{-\left(1-e^{-\|x-y\|^2}\right)\right\}
 is completely monotone (and hence PD).
We call this the Exp–Exp kernel.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Big Picture Idea
For a given loss \ell, the regression task is

\inf_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \, \mathbb{E}[\ell(f(X), Y)],

seeking functions f with good predictive performance.
Performance depends on

Choice of loss (e.g. squared error, cross-entropy),
Choice of hypothesis class \mathcal{F} (linear models, kernels, neural networks),
Choice of regularisation (norm constraints, weight decay, spectral penalties).

Successful methods exploit inductive biases matched to data geometry. E.g. CNNs for images, GNNs for graphs, transformers for sequences, etc.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Fourier Regression
Fourier viewpoint
Any f \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d) has the Fourier representation

f(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \hat f(\theta) \, e^{-i \theta^\top x} \, d\theta,

where \hat f encodes the spectral content of f. In practice, we cannot learn \hat f directly, but we can approximate f by truncating or discretising the integral:

f(x) \approx \sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_j e^{-i \theta_j^\top x},

with frequencies {\theta_j} drawn either adaptively or at random. This turns regression into learning coefficients in a Fourier basis.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Fourier Regression
Why Fourier?
Fourier analysis is the harmonic analysis associated with the geometry of Euclidean space:

\mathbb{R}^d is a locally compact abelian (LCA) group under addition.
Its Haar measure is the Lebesgue measure, the unique shift-invariant measure.
By Pontryagin duality, the characters of this group are the exponentials e^{-i \theta^\top x}, and the Fourier transform is the corresponding Gelfand transform.

Thus, the Fourier basis encodes translation symmetry - the fundamental symmetry of Euclidean space.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Fourier Regression
Generalisations and Connections
There are analogous Fourier transforms on different LCA groups:

On \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} the dual group gives the Discrete Fourier Transform.
On the torus \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}, it yields the Fourier series.
On the p-adic numbers \mathbb{Q}_p, there is a corresponding Fourier transform (discussed later).
More generally, shift-invariant kernels admit a Fourier spectral representation (Bochner’s theorem). This underlies random Fourier features and spectral kernel methods.

So “Fourier regression” is not just heuristic: it’s a principled basis expansion matched to the group structure of the data, with natural regularisation in the frequency domain (e.g. penalising high frequencies).
It encodes the inductive bias of shift-invariance.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Variational Fourier Regression


How do we learn \hat{f}(\theta)?
Have been working on variational objectives: 
\mathcal{F}(Q) = \underbrace{\mathcal{L}(Q)}_{\text{Loss}} + \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}(Q \| Q_0)}_{\text{Regulariser}},

where

▶ Q is a probability distribution
▶ Q_0 is a prior

This general objective includes: Bayesian inference, prediction centric inference, and more! Different methods:
Particle Based Methods

▶ Mean-Field Langevin Dynamics
▶ Generalisations of SVGD
▶ Fisher-Rao geometries e.g. mirror descent

Parametric Methods

▶ Normalising flows
▶ Mixtures of Gaussians (e.g. this paper)

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Issues
We might want to treat \hat f (the Fourier transform of f) as a probability measure so that we can plug it directly into the variational framework.
However:

\hat f is not generally a probability measure.

It can be complex-valued, can have negative parts, and is not normalised.
Only in special cases (e.g. positive-definite functions, characteristic functions of distributions) can \hat f be directly interpreted as a probability law.

If we force it into a probability-measure framework, then we are really heading in the direction of Bochner’s theorem: representing kernels as expectations over Fourier features.

In this case, \hat f is no longer “the Fourier transform of the predictor” but is instead treated as a spectral measure that defines a kernel.
Optimising over such spectral measures corresponds to kernel learning, not direct function learning.


Comparing with Random Fourier Features
By Bochner’s theorem: If k(x-y) is a continuous, normalised (k(0) = 1), stationary, positive-definite kernel on \mathbb{R}^d, then there exists a probability measure \lambda on \mathbb{R}^d such that

k(x,y) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{i \theta^\top(x-y)} \, d\lambda(\theta).


\lambda is called the spectral measure.
If k is real-valued, \lambda must be symmetric \lambda(A)=\lambda(-A).

Random Fourier Features (RFF) approximate this integral via Monte Carlo:

k(x,y) \approx \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^m \cos(\theta_j^\top(x-y)), \quad \theta_j \sim \lambda.

If you plug this approximation into Kernel Ridge Regression, the predictor has the form

f(x) = w^\top \phi(x),

where

\phi(x) = \big(\cos(\theta_1^\top x), \ldots, \cos(\theta_m^\top x)\big).


The weights w \in \mathbb{R}^m are learned by minimising the regression loss (ridge regression in this finite-dimensional feature space).
The frequencies {\theta_j} are usually fixed after the initial sampling from \lambda, though some variants learn/adapt them.

Desiderata
To create a novel approach (I think), we want to:

Treat \hat{f} as a function or signed measure
Optimise \hat{f} in an analogous framework

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Gradient flows on Riemannian Manifolds
Gradient flows in Euclidean Space
For a functional F:\mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R, the gradient flow is 
\dot x_t = -\nabla F(x_t).
 This is “steepest descent” with respect to the Euclidean inner product \langle u,v\rangle=\sum u_i v_i.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Gradient flows on Riemannian Manifolds
Generalising to a Riemannian manifold
Let (\mathcal M,g) be a Riemannian manifold:

At each point p\in\mathcal M, the tangent space T_p\mathcal M is a vector space of admissible directions.
The metric tensor g_p: T_p\mathcal M\times T_p\mathcal M\to \mathbb R is an inner product that can vary with p.

Gradient of F: the vector \nabla^g F(p)\in T_p\mathcal M such that 
dF(p)[\xi] = g_p(\nabla^g F(p), \xi) \quad\forall \xi\in T_p\mathcal M,
 where dF is the differential (directional derivative).
Gradient flow: the ODE 
\partial_t p_t = -\nabla^g F(p_t), \quad p_t\in\mathcal M.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Gradient flows on Riemannian Manifolds
Role of tangent space choice

The definition of T_p\mathcal M tells you what counts as a direction.
Example: in Wasserstein geometry, tangent vectors at a measure Q are velocity fields; in an embedding geometry, tangents are embedding perturbations.

Different tangent models give different possible evolutions.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Gradient flows on Riemannian Manifolds
Role of the metric tensor

The metric tensor tells you how to measure the size and angle of tangent vectors.
“Steepest descent” is always defined relative to this inner product.
Changing the metric changes the gradient direction.

Example:

With Euclidean metric, gradient is just \nabla F.
With a preconditioned metric g(u,v)=u^\top M v, the gradient becomes M^{-1}\nabla F.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Gradient flows on Riemannian Manifolds
Exponential map and evolution
Once you have a tangent vector v\in T_p\mathcal M, you evolve by following the geodesic starting at p with velocity v. This is the exponential map: 
p' = \exp_p(v).

So the evolution rule depends jointly on:

How you define tangents (what’s allowed),
How you measure them (the metric tensor), and
How you “integrate them back” to the manifold (the exponential map).

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
What is SVGD?
Suppose we want to optimise the objective:

\mathcal{F}(Q) = \underbrace{\mathcal{L}(Q)}_{\text{Loss}} + \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}(Q \| Q_0)}_{\text{Regulariser}}.

A natural idea would be to consider a Riemannian manifold of probability measures and perform a gradient flow.
To recover SVGD we use the Riemannian manifold of W_2 with the tangent space given by Stein RKHS directions.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
What is SVGD?
Wasserstein W_2 Space (Otto construction)
Consider the Wasserstein-2 space: 
W_2(\mathbb{R}^d) = \left\{ P \ \text{probability measure on } \mathbb{R}^d \mid \int |x|^2 dP(x) < \infty \right\}.


Tangent space at P: 
\mathcal{T}_P W_2 = \{ -\nabla \cdot (P v) \mid v \in L^2(P;\mathbb{R}^d) \}.

Exponential map: pushing forward P by a transport map 
\exp_P(v) = (I + \varepsilon v)_\# P.

Riemannian metric: 
g_P(v,w) = \int v(x)\cdot w(x) \, dP(x).


This equips W_2 with a formal Riemannian structure (the Otto calculus).

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
What is SVGD?
Gradient Flow in W_2
Given a functional \mathcal{F}: W_2 \to \mathbb{R}, the Wasserstein gradient flow satisfies: 
\partial_t P_t = - \nabla \cdot \left(P_t \, \nabla \frac{\delta \mathcal{F}}{\delta P}(x)\right),
 where \frac{\delta \mathcal{F}}{\delta P} is the first variation of \mathcal{F}.
This is a PDE describing the evolution of measures under steepest descent in Wasserstein space.
Why not just use this?
In practice, directly solving this PDE is intractable. Instead, SVGD takes a particle approximation: 
Q \approx \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_{x_i}.

We then evolve the particles x_i along a velocity field v chosen to maximally decrease \mathcal{F}.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
What is SVGD?
Kernelised Stein Gradient
SVGD chooses v from a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) \mathcal{H}^d of vector fields with kernel k.

Stein’s identity ensures that the optimal direction of steepest descent can be expressed in closed form in this RKHS.
The resulting particle dynamics are: 
x_i \leftarrow x_i + \varepsilon \, \phi^*(x_i),
 with update function 
\phi^*(\cdot) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim Q}\big[ \nabla_x \log \pi(x) \, k(x,\cdot) + \nabla_x k(x,\cdot) \big],
 where \pi is the target distribution (often \pi \propto e^{-\mathcal{L}}).

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Option 1: Reparameterise
Rewrite our regressors as:
\begin{align*}
f(x) &= \int \hat{f}(\theta) e^{-i \theta^\top x} \,\mathrm{d}\theta \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim Q} \left[ a(\theta) e^{-i \theta^\top x}  \right].
\end{align*}
Effectively decomposes the inverse Fourier transform as:

\hat{f}(\theta) = \mathrm{d}Q(\theta) \, a(\theta).

Issues:

A vanilla approach (boring)
Need to learn a as well.
Effectively just learning a mixture distribution Q (similar to current/previous work).
The regressor just becomes a product of a(\theta) and a two-layer neural network with cosine activation (but with an interpretation as a spectral mixture).

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Option 2: Two Particle “Swarms”
Treat \hat{f} as a signed measure and use the Hahn-Jordan decomposition to write: 
\hat{f} = a\, Q^+ - b \, Q^-,
 where Q^+ and Q^- are probability measures and a,b \geq 0 are non-negative constants. To implement this:

Treat both Q^+ and Q^- as empirical measures 
Q^+ = \sum_{i=1}^m w^+_i \delta_{\theta^+_i}, \quad Q^{-} = \sum_{j = 1}^M w^-_j \delta_{\theta^-_j},

First take a step to evolve Q^+ then a step to evolve Q^- and then a vanilla Euclidean GD on (a,b) (with operator splitting).

Issues:

Nice idea but seems annoying to implement (and figure out the details)
Doubles number of hyperparameters

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Option 3: RKHS Descent
Entirely abandon forcing a probability measure and W_2. Instead, we optimise directly over a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS)!



Note: We could’ve just used L^2 instead, but an analogue of SVGD does not follow…



Let k be a PSD kernel with RKHS \mathcal{H}(k). Any signed measure \nu can be embedded in the RKHS via 
\mu_\nu(\cdot) = \int k(\theta, \cdot) \,\mathrm{d}\nu(\theta)

which induces a norm 
\| \nu \|_{\mathcal{H}(k)} = \iint k(\theta, \theta') \,\mathrm{d}\nu(\theta) \,\mathrm{d}\nu(\theta').

\mathcal{H}(k) is a Riemannian manifold with tangent space \mathcal{H}(k).
Let’s figure out the details!

text:
Evolution
To evolve the original objective, break it down into constituent components:

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
\mathcal{L}(\nu) update derivation (can skip)

Parameter space \Theta and a PD kernel k:\Theta\times\Theta\to\mathbb R with RKHS \mathcal H_k.
For a finite signed measure \nu on \Theta, its kernel mean embedding is 
\mu_\nu(\cdot)=\int k(\cdot,\theta)\,d\nu(\theta)\in\mathcal H_k.

For a signed variation h, the corresponding embedding variation is 
\mu_h(\cdot) = \int k(\cdot,\theta)\,dh(\theta)\in\mathcal H_k.


We want to descend a functional \mathcal L(\nu). Define \tilde{\mathcal L}(\mu):=\mathcal L(\nu) with \mu=\mu_\nu.
Riemannian (RKHS) gradient
We use the Hilbert structure of \mathcal H_k. The Riemannian gradient G_\nu\in\mathcal H_k is the unique element such that 
\langle G_\nu,\mu_h\rangle_{\mathcal H_k}\;=\;D\mathcal L(\nu)[h]\quad\forall h.

This is the Riesz representation of the Fréchet derivative of \tilde{\mathcal L} at \mu_\nu.

If a pointwise functional derivative \psi_\nu exists with 
D\mathcal L(\nu)[h]=\int \psi_\nu(\theta)\,dh(\theta),
 then 
\langle G_\nu,\mu_h\rangle=\int G_\nu(\theta)\,dh(\theta)=\int \psi_\nu(\theta)\,dh(\theta),
 which implies

G_\nu=\Pi_{\mathcal H_k} \psi_\nu,
 the orthogonal projection of \psi_\nu onto \mathcal H_k.
In general, G_\nu is simply the Riesz representer; the pointwise description is optional.

Thus the gradient flow is 
\partial_t \mu_{\nu_t}=-G_{\nu_t}.

Particle form
Let \nu=\sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_j \delta_{\theta_j}. Then 
\mu_\nu = \sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_j k(\cdot,\theta_j).

If particles move, then (assuming k is C^1 in its second argument) 
\partial_t \mu_\nu
=\sum_j \dot\alpha_j\,k(\cdot,\theta_j)\;+\;\sum_j \alpha_j\,\nabla_{\theta_j} k(\cdot,\theta_j)\cdot \dot\theta_j.
\tag{★}

Galerkin system
Define nodal data 
g_i := G_\nu(\theta_i)=\langle G_\nu, k(\cdot,\theta_i)\rangle = D\mathcal L(\nu)[\delta_{\theta_i}].

Let 
K_{ij}=k(\theta_i,\theta_j),\qquad
B_{m:}(\theta,\alpha)=\Big[\sum_j \alpha_j \nabla_{\theta_j}k(\theta_m,\theta_j)\Big]^\top.

Projecting \partial_t\mu_\nu=-G_\nu against k(\cdot,\theta_m) gives 
K\dot\alpha+B(\theta,\alpha)\dot\theta=-g.
\tag{GS}

This expresses the orthogonal projection of the infinite-dimensional gradient onto the tangent space of the finite-dimensional particle manifold.
Choices of update

Weight-only update (exact in span). 
\boxed{\;\dot\alpha=-K^{-1}g,\quad \dot\theta=0.\;}
 This exactly matches the projected gradient using only weight changes.
Location-only update (natural gradient). Fix \dot\alpha=0 and solve least squares for \dot\theta: 
\boxed{\;\dot\theta=-(B^\top B+\lambda I)^{-1}B^\top g,\;}
 with small \lambda>0 for damping.
Joint update. Solve 
\min_{\dot\alpha,\dot\theta}\ \|K\dot\alpha+B\dot\theta+g\|_2^2
 (optionally with Tikhonov). This gives the least-squares projection of the ambient gradient.

Why approximate in \mathrm{span}\{k(\cdot,\theta_i)\}?
The manifold 
\mathcal M_m=\Big\{\sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_j k(\cdot,\theta_j)\Big\}\subset\mathcal H_k
 is the finite-dimensional submanifold of the RKHS induced by m particles.
When we restrict optimisation to this manifold, we are not free to move in arbitrary directions of \mathcal H_k: the only admissible variations are those that come from perturbing the particle weights \alpha_j or their locations \theta_j.
Tangent space structure
The tangent space at \mu_\nu\in\mathcal M_m is 
T_{\mu_\nu}\mathcal M_m
=\mathrm{span}\big\{\,k(\cdot,\theta_j)\,\}_{j=1}^m \;\cup\; \{\,\nabla_{\theta_j}k(\cdot,\theta_j)\,\}_{j=1}^m.


Moving \alpha_j perturbs \mu_\nu in the direction k(\cdot,\theta_j).
Moving \theta_j perturbs \mu_\nu in the direction \nabla_{\theta_j}k(\cdot,\theta_j).

Thus the only directions available to us lie in this span.
Gradient projection
The ambient RKHS gradient G_\nu may not belong to T_{\mu_\nu}\mathcal M_m.
The correct Riemannian gradient on the submanifold is its orthogonal projection: 
\nabla^{\mathcal M_m}\mathcal L(\mu_\nu)
=\Pi_{T_{\mu_\nu}\mathcal M_m}(G_\nu).
 This is a geometric fact: gradient flows are always tangent to the manifold they evolve on.
Collocation / interpolation step
Practically, we often restrict further to the weight span \mathrm{span}\{k(\cdot,\theta_j)\}, ignoring the derivative directions.
In this case, the best approximation of G_\nu in this span is the minimum-norm kernel interpolant \hat G that matches the nodal values 
g_i := G_\nu(\theta_i).
 By standard RKHS theory (the representer/interpolation property), 
\hat G(\cdot)=\sum_{j=1}^m \beta_j k(\cdot,\theta_j),\qquad \beta=K^{-1}g,
 where K_{ij}=k(\theta_i,\theta_j).
This identity is exactly the projection of G_\nu onto the span \{k(\cdot,\theta_j)\} expressed in collocation form.

text:
SKL update derivation (can skip)
For sufficiently smooth vector valued \phi, can show that for T_\varepsilon = \mathrm{Id} + \varepsilon \phi: 
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \mathrm{KL}((T_\varepsilon)_\# \mu \| Q) \Big\lvert_{\varepsilon = 0} = \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim \mu}\left[ \mathcal{S}_Q \, \phi(\theta) \right],
 where 
\mathcal{S}_Q \phi =  \nabla \log q \cdot \phi + \nabla \cdot \phi
 is the vector-valued Stein operator.
Applying this to each Hahn-Jordan part of \nu and \nu_0 we have

\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \mathrm{SKL}((T_\varepsilon)_\# \nu \| \nu_0) \Big\lvert_{\varepsilon = 0} = \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim \nu^+}\left[ \mathcal{S}_{\nu_0^+} \, \phi(\theta) \right] + \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim \nu^-}\left[ \mathcal{S}_{\nu^-_0} \, \phi(\theta) \right].

For particles:

\nu = \sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_j \delta_{\theta_j},

define the sign-index sets and (unnormalised) Hahn–Jordan weights 
J_+ := \{\, j : \alpha_j>0 \,\},\quad
J_- := \{\, j : \alpha_j<0 \,\},\quad
\alpha_j^{+} := \max(\alpha_j,0),\quad
\alpha_j^{-} := \max(-\alpha_j,0).

with 
w_j^{+}=\frac{\alpha_j^{+}}{\sum_{\ell\in J_+}\alpha_\ell^{+}},
\qquad
w_j^{-}=\frac{\alpha_j^{-}}{\sum_{\ell\in J_-}\alpha_\ell^{-}},
 yielding \begin{align*}
\dot{\theta}_i &= -\mathbf{1}_{\{ i\in J_+ \}}
\sum_{\ell\in J_+}\tilde w_\ell^{+}\Big(
k(\theta_i,\theta_\ell)\,\nabla \log \nu_0^{+}(\theta_\ell)
+\nabla_{\theta_\ell} k(\theta_i,\theta_\ell)
\Big) \\
&\quad -\mathbf{1}_{\{ i\in J_- \}}
\sum_{\ell\in J_-}\tilde w_\ell^{-}\Big(
k(\theta_i,\theta_\ell)\,\nabla \log \nu_0^{-}(\theta_\ell)
+\nabla_{\theta_\ell} k(\theta_i,\theta_\ell)
\Big).
\end{align*}
For an RBF kernel k(\theta,\theta')=\exp(-|\theta-\theta'|^2/(2\ell^2)), 
\nabla_{\theta_\ell}k(\theta_i,\theta_\ell)=\frac{1}{\ell^2},k(\theta_i,\theta_\ell),(\theta_i-\theta_\ell),
 so the update simplifies to 
\dot{\theta}_i
= -\sum_{\ell\in J_{\operatorname{sign}(\alpha_i)}}\tilde w_\ell^{(\operatorname{sign})}
k(\theta_i,\theta_\ell)\left[
\nabla \log \nu^{(\operatorname{sign})}(\theta_\ell)
+\frac{1}{\ell^2}(\theta_i-\theta_\ell)
\right].

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
p-adic numbers
For a prime p, the p-adic absolute value on \mathbb{Q} is 
|x|_p=\begin{cases}
p^{-k}\, & x=p^k\frac{a}{b},\; a,b\in\mathbb{Z}, \; p\nmid a,b, \\
0,& x=0.
\end{cases}
 Numbers divisible by many powers of p are small p-adically (e.g. |8|_2=2^{-3}).
Let v_p(x)\in\mathbb{Z}\cup{\infty} be the p-adic valuation (largest k with p^k\mid x and v_p(0)=\infty). Then |x|_p=p^{-v_p(x)} and 
|x+y|_p \le \max\{|x|_p,|y|_p\}\quad\text{(ultrametric inequality).}

Completions. The completion of \mathbb{Q} under |\cdot|_p is \mathbb{Q}_p. Elements have expansions 
x=\sum_{i=k_0}^{\infty} a_i p^i, \qquad a_i\in\{0,\dots,p-1\}, \; k_0\in\mathbb{Z},
 i.e. only finitely many negative powers occur; for \mathbb{Z}_p (the compact open unit ball) we have k_0\ge 0.
Balls and measure. Closed balls are cosets a+p^m\mathbb{Z}_p. With Haar measure \mu normalised by \mu(\mathbb{Z}_p)=1, one has \mu(a+p^m\mathbb{Z}_p)=p^{-m}.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Hierarchical data and p-adics
The ultrametric induces a tree: each ball a+p^m\mathbb{Z}_p splits into p disjoint children a+bp^m+p^{m+1}\mathbb{Z}_p, b\in{0,\dots,p-1}. Two points are close iff they agree to many leading base-p digits: 
v_p(x-y)=\text{length of the longest common prefix of the $p$-adic digit strings of $x,y$.}

Canonical encodings.

Binary/quad strings (e.g. taxonomy, DNA): choose p=2 or p=4. Encode a finite string s=(s_0,\dots,s_{L-1}) as x=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1} s_i p^i\in\mathbb{Z}_p. Then 
v_p(x-x')=\min{i: s_i\neq s_i'}\quad(\text{or } \infty \text{ if identical}),
 so distance equals first divergence depth in the tree.
General rooted trees of out-degree \le p: label edges 0,\dots,p-1 from root and encode the path label as above.

This makes \mathbb{Q}_p a natural host for clustering, phylogenies, and any prefix-based similarity.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Fourier transform (p-adic Fourier analysis)
Consider the LCA group (\mathbb{Q}_p,+) with Haar measure \mu (\mu(\mathbb{Z}_p)=1). Fix the standard additive character \psi:\mathbb{Q}_p\to\mathbb{T} that is trivial on \mathbb{Z}_p and non-trivial on p^{-1}\mathbb{Z}_p (concretely, \psi(x)=e^{2\pi i {x}_p}, where {x}_p\in\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z} is determined by the finitely many negative-power digits of x).

Fourier/Gelfand transform: 
\widehat{f}(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{Q}_p} f(x)\,\psi(\xi x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad \xi\in\mathbb{Q}_p.

Inversion/Plancherel (with dual Haar d\xi): 
f(x)=\int_{\mathbb{Q}_p} \widehat{f}(\xi)\,\psi(-\xi x)\,d\xi\,\qquad |f|_2=|\widehat f|_2.

Characters. Every continuous character is \chi_\xi(x)=\psi(\xi x) for a unique \xi\in\mathbb{Q}_p; the dual group is \widehat{\mathbb{Q}}_p\cong\mathbb{Q}_p.

Practical evaluation. If computations are at resolution m (finite strings/digits), then 
\chi_\xi(x)=\exp\Big(2\pi i \;\frac{(\xi x)\bmod p^m}{p^m}\Big),
 so you only need modular arithmetic on integers of size p^m.
