title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Big picture
Goal: Generate high-quality (ideally independent) samples from a target density \pi.
Standard Approaches:

MCMC produces asymptotically exact samples but with autocorrelation; thinning/post-processing is usually required.
SVGD (Stein Variational Gradient Descent) gives deterministic, interacting particles with built-in repulsion, but needs a differentiable score \nabla\log\pi and often struggles on multimodal targets.

Idea: For any \pi-invariant Markov kernel P (or generator \mathcal{A}) we:

take its Stein operator T_\pi,
build the Stein RKHS geometry induced by a kernel k,
construct an analogue of SVGD

This yields a generalised SVGD whose update is a “particle version” of the given MCMC—preserving invariance while adding SVGD style repulsion. With Metropolis–Hastings (MH), you get a Stein-tilted MH step that remains \pi-invariant but encourages diversity.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Aside: Stein Operators
A Stein operator for a target \pi is any operator T_\pi such that

\mathbb{E}_{X\sim \pi}[ (T_\pi f)(X)] = 0.

There are three kinds of “Stein” operators which can make things confusing:

Generators on scalars: An operator \mathcal{A}_\pi which takes in scalar-valued functions and outputs scalar-valued functions.

\mathcal{A}_\pi f = \nabla \cdot \nabla f + \nabla\log\pi \cdot \nabla f

Vector to scalar: An operator \mathcal{S}_\pi which takes in vector-valued functions and outputs scalar-valued functions. 
\mathcal{S}_\pi \phi = \nabla \cdot \phi + \nabla\log\pi \cdot \phi.

Scalar to vector (Stein feature operator): An operator \mathcal{G}_\pi which takes in scalar-valued functions and outputs vector valued functions. 
\mathcal{G}_\pi f = \nabla f + f \, \nabla \log \pi.


They are related:

\mathcal{A}_\pi f = \mathcal{S}_\pi (\nabla f) = \nabla \cdot (\mathcal{G}_\pi f).

Creating Stein Operators
A natural way to construct a Stein operator is through Markov processes which leave the target \pi invariant.
Discrete Time
For a discrete time \pi-invariant Markov process with Markov kernel P, we can define the Markov-Stein operator associated with P:

(T_\pi f)(x) \coloneqq (P f)(x)-f(x).

It satisfies the Stein identity \mathbb E_\pi[T_\pi f]=0 for bounded measurable f since \pi P = \pi and \int P f\,\mathrm{d}\pi = \int f\,\mathrm{d}\pi.
Continuous Time
In a continuous time \pi-invariant Markov process, we can construct a Stein operator via the semigroup or its generator:

Semigroup: Define \mathcal{S}_t f := P_t f - f, with (P_t)_{t\geq 0} a \pi invariant semigroup. Then 
  \mathbb{E}_\pi[\mathcal{S}_t f] = \int (P_t f - f) \, d\pi = 0,
  
Generator: Define \mathcal{S}_\pi := \mathcal{A} with \mathcal{A} a \pi invariant generator, then 
\mathbb{E}_\pi[\mathcal{S}_\pi f] = \mathbb{E}_\pi[\mathcal{A} f] = \mathbb{E}_\pi\left[\lim_{t\to 0^+} \frac{P_t f - f}{t}\right] = 0.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Introduction to Vanilla SVGD
Let \pi be a target density on \mathbb{R}^d and Q a current approximation. The KL divergence is:

\mathrm{KL}(Q \| \pi) = \int \log\left(\frac{dQ}{d\pi}\right) \,\mathrm{d}Q.

Consider the infinitesimal transport T_\varepsilon(x)=x+\varepsilon\,\phi(x) with a vector field \phi:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d. We choose \phi to maximise the instantaneous decrease of KL:

\min_{\phi}\ \left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \mathrm{KL}\big((T_\varepsilon)_\# Q \| \pi\big)\right|_{\varepsilon=0}.

By a calculation involving change of variables and a Taylor series expansion of the density of (T_\varepsilon)_\# Q, it can be shown:

\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \left.\mathrm{KL}( (T_\varepsilon)_\# Q \| \pi  )\right|_{\varepsilon = 0} = -\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}\left[ (\mathcal{S}_\pi \phi)(X) \right],

where \mathcal{S}_\pi \phi = \phi \cdot \nabla \log \pi  + \nabla\cdot\phi.
Now restrict \phi to the vector-valued RKHS 
\mathcal H_K = \bigoplus_{i=1}^d \mathcal H_k,
\qquad K(z,x)=k(z,x)\,I_d,
 where k:\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R} is a scalar positive-definite kernel and I_d is the d\times d identity. Using the reproducing properties in \mathcal H_K, the functional \phi \mapsto \mathbb{E}_Q[\mathcal{S}_\pi \phi] has Riesz representer 
\boxed{\;
\Phi_Q(z) = \mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}\left[k(z,X)\nabla\log\pi(X) + \nabla_X k(z,X)\right].
\;}
 where \nabla_X k(z,X) denotes the gradient of k w.r.t. its second argument.
Then, since \mathcal{H}_K is a Hilbert space, Cauchy-Schwarz tells us:

-\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \left.\mathrm{KL}( (T_\varepsilon)_\# Q \| \pi  )\right|_{\varepsilon = 0} = \mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}\left[ (\mathcal{S}_\pi \phi)(X) \right] = \langle \phi, \Phi_Q \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_K} \leq \|\phi\|_{\mathcal{H}_K} \|\Phi_Q\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}.

We wish to maximise this. Therefore, the steepest descent direction over the unit ball is \phi^* = \tfrac{\Phi_Q}{\|\Phi_Q\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}}. In practice we use the field 
\boxed{\;\phi_{\text{SVGD}}(z) = \Phi_Q(z)
=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}\left[k(z,X)\nabla\log\pi(X) + \nabla_X k(z,X)\right].}

A single Euler step updates particles x_i\leftarrow x_i+\eta\,\phi_{\text{SVGD}}(x_i). Moreover, 
\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\ \mathrm{KL}\big((T_\varepsilon)_\# Q  \| \pi\big) \right|_{\varepsilon = 0}
= -\|\Phi_Q\|_{\mathcal H_K}^2,
 i.e. the squared kernel Stein discrepancy (KSD) equals the instantaneous KL decrease along \phi_{\text{SVGD}}.
Empirical form: With particles \{x_j\}_{j=1}^n defining an empirical measure Q = \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n \delta_{x_j}, the SVGD update becomes: 
\phi_{\text{SVGD}}(z) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n \Big[k(z,x_j)\,\nabla\log\pi(x_j) + \nabla_{x_j} k(z,x_j)\Big].

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
The (rough) Generalisation
In vanilla SVGD, the “Stein field” was 
\phi_{\text{SVGD}}(z)
=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}\left[k(z,X)\nabla\log\pi(X) + \nabla_X k(z,X)\right] = \mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\mathcal{G}_\pi^X k(z,X)],
 where (\mathcal{G}_\pi f)(x) = f(x) \nabla\log\pi(x) + \nabla f(x) is the scalar \to vector Stein feature operator.
For a Markov-Stein operator \mathcal{S}_P f = Pf - f, this implies we want something like:

\phi_{P\text{-SVGD}}(z) = \mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\mathcal{S}_P^X k(z,X)].

Issues

As written, the \phi_{P\text{-SVGD}}(z) is not a transport map - it is scalar-valued!
Even if it did make sense, how can it be justified?
The derivation of the standard SVGD assumed the use of KL divergence and transports of the form 
T_\varepsilon = \mathrm{Id} + \varepsilon\,\phi.

With these assumptions, the Langevin Stein operator \mathcal{S}_\pi appeared.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Alternative View
Instead of considering a transport map to move Q, we consider a family of Markov kernels:

\{ P_{\varepsilon} \mid -\epsilon_0 \leq \varepsilon \leq \epsilon_0, \; P_0 = P \}.

Define

F(\varepsilon) = \mathrm{KL}(Q \, P_\varepsilon \| \pi ).

We seek the Markov kernel which maximises the instaneous decrease of KL:

F'(0) = \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \left. \mathrm{KL}(Q \, P_\varepsilon \| \pi ) \right|_{\varepsilon = 0}.

Constraints on P_\varepsilon
Let (P_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon} be a family of Markov kernels with P_0=P. For bounded measurable f, write 
(P_\varepsilon f)(x)=\int f(y)\,P_\varepsilon(x,dy).
 If the map \varepsilon\mapsto P_\varepsilon f is differentiable at 0 for all bounded f, define the signed kernel derivative M by 
(M f)(x)\;:=\;\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\,(P_\varepsilon f)(x)\right|_{\varepsilon=0}.
 By Riesz–Markov, this means that for each fixed x, there exists a finite signed measure M(x,\cdot) on the state space so that 
(M f)(x)=\int f(y)\,M(x,dy).

Intuitively: P_\varepsilon = P + \varepsilon M + o(\varepsilon) in the weak sense.
Now differentiate the standard identities:
Stochasticity (row sums =1).
For every \varepsilon and x, \int P_\varepsilon(x,dy)=1. Differentiate at 0: 
\int M(x,dy)=0\quad\text{for all }x
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
M\, 1 =0.

\pi-invariance to first order.
If P_\varepsilon leaves \pi invariant for all \varepsilon, then for every bounded f, 
\int (P_\varepsilon f)(x)\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x)=\int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x).
 Differentiate at 0: 
\int (M f)(x)\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x)=0\quad\text{for all }f.
 Equivalently, as a signed measure in y, 
\int M(x,dy)\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x)=0
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\pi M=0.

Reversibility (detailed balance) to first order.
If each P_\varepsilon is \pi-reversible, then for all measurable sets A,B: 
\int_A\!\!\int_B \mathrm{d}\pi(x)\,P_\varepsilon(x,dy)
=
\int_A\!\!\int_B \pi(dy)\,P_\varepsilon(y,dx).
 Differentiate at 0 and use symmetry in (A,B) to get, as measures on \mathcal X\times\mathcal X, 
\pi(dx)\,M(x,dy)\;=\;\pi(dy)\,M(y,dx).
 This is the “detailed balance at first order”.
Parameterising P_\varepsilon
Assume P is \pi-reversible and set 
\mu(dx,dy):=\pi(dx)\,P(x,dy).
 Then \mu is symmetric: \mu(dx,dy)=\mu(dy,dx).
A class of perturbations is obtained by weighting the jump x\to y with a function A(x,y) and compensating on the diagonal so rows still sum to zero: 
(Mf)(x)=\int\big(f(y)-f(x)\big)\,A(x,y)\,P(x,dy).
 Equivalently, as (signed) kernels, 
M(x,dy)=A(x,y)\,P(x,dy)\;-\;\Big[\int A(x,z)\,P(x,dz)\Big]\,\delta_x(dy).
\tag{†}

Let’s check the three constraints and see what symmetry of A is forced:
Row sums. With f\equiv 1, (Mf)(x)=\int(1-1)\,A(\cdot)\,P=0. So M\mathbf 1=0 holds for any A.
\pi-invariance at first order. For any f, 
\int (Mf)(x)\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x)=\iint \big(f(y)-f(x)\big)\,A(x,y)\,\mu(dx,dy).
 Swap (x,y) and use symmetry of \mu to see this integral is the negative of itself, hence 0 regardless of the symmetry of A. Thus \pi M=0 always holds.
Reversibility at first order. Here the symmetry of A matters. From (†), 
\pi(dx)\,M(x,dy)=A(x,y)\,\mu(dx,dy)\;-\;\pi(dx)\,a(x)\,\delta_x(dy),
\qquad a(x):=\int A(x,z)\,P(x,dz).
 Swapping (x,y) we obtain \pi(dy)\,M(y,dx)=A(y,x)\,\mu(dx,dy)-\pi(dy)\,a(y)\,\delta_y(dx). For these two signed measures to be equal, we must have on the off-diagonal (where \delta-terms vanish) 
A(x,y)\,\mu(dx,dy)=A(y,x)\,\mu(dx,dy)
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
A(x,y)=A(y,x)\quad(\mu\text{-a.e.}).
 The diagonal compensation terms then match automatically.
Conclusion: to preserve reversibility to first order, A must be symmetric \mu-a.e.

title: Variational Fourier Regression
text:
Derivation
Step 1: Gâteaux derivative of \mathrm{KL}
Let Q\ll \pi with density \rho=\dfrac{dQ}{d\pi} and 
\mathrm{KL}(Q\|\pi)=\int \rho\log\rho\,d\pi.
 Consider a differentiable path of probability measures (Q_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon} with Q_0=Q and 
\dot Q := \left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} Q_\varepsilon \right|_{\varepsilon=0},
\qquad \dot Q(\mathcal X)=0.
 Assume Q_\varepsilon\ll\pi for |\varepsilon| small with densities \rho_\varepsilon=\dfrac{dQ_\varepsilon}{d\pi} differentiable at \varepsilon=0 \pi-a.e., and \dot\rho:=\left.\dfrac{d}{d\varepsilon}\rho_\varepsilon \right|_{\varepsilon=0}. Then d\dot q=\dot\rho\,d\pi.
Write \varphi(t)=t\log t. Then \varphi'(t)=1+\log t and 
F(\varepsilon):=\mathrm{KL}(Q_\varepsilon\|\pi)=\int \varphi(\rho_\varepsilon)\,d\pi.
 By differentiation under the integral sign: 
F'(0)=\int \varphi'(\rho)\,\dot\rho\,d\pi
=\int \bigl(1+\log\rho\bigr)\,d\dot Q.
 Because \dot Q(\mathcal X)=\int 1\,d\dot Q=0, the constant “1” drops out: 
F'(0)=\int \log\rho\,d\dot Q
=\int \log\!\Big(\frac{dQ}{d\pi}\Big)\,d\dot Q.

Step 2: What is the allowable \dot q?
Given a current law Q, the one–step pushforward along P_\varepsilon is Q_\varepsilon:=Q\,P_\varepsilon. Its tangent is 
\dot Q
:=\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\, Q\,P_\varepsilon\right|_{\varepsilon=0}
= QM,
\qquad\text{i.e.}\quad
\langle f,\dot Q\rangle
=\int (Mf)(x)\,Q(dx).

Using the property of M: 
\boxed{\;
\langle f,\dot q\rangle
=\iint \big(f(y)-f(x)\big)\,A(x,y)\,\underbrace{q(dx)\,P(x,dy)}_{=:~\mu_Q(dx,dy)}\;.
}
\tag{Tangent}
 Here \mu_q is the one–step coupling of (Q,P). Note \mu_q is generally not symmetric unless Q=\pi.
Step 3: First variation of \mathrm{KL}
The Gâteaux derivative of KL gives 
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\left.\mathrm{KL}(Q\,P_\varepsilon\|\pi) \right|_{\varepsilon=0}
=\int \log\!\Big(\frac{dQ}{d\pi}\Big)\,d\dot Q
=\left\langle \log\dfrac{dQ}{d\pi},\dot Q\right\rangle.
 Therefore: 
\boxed{\;
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\Big|_{\varepsilon=0}\mathrm{KL}(Q\,P_\varepsilon\|\pi)
= \iint \big(\log\dfrac{dQ}{d\pi}(y)-\log\dfrac{dQ}{d\pi}(x)\big)\,A(x,y)\,\mu_Q(dx,dy)\;.
}

This is the general first–order formula for any admissible perturbation (i.e. any symmetric A in (\dagger)).
